title: Chemical profiling, bioactivity, and machine learning-supported target analysis of  Euphorbia macroclada  extracts from aerial parts and roots
content: Euphorbia macroclada is used in Anatolian folk medicine, but its chemistry and bioactivity have not been compared across plant parts and extraction solvents. We extracted aerial parts and roots with ethyl acetate, acetone, 70% aqueous acetone and water. The extracts were then profiled by LC-MS/MS and tested in antioxidant and enzyme inhibition assays. UHPLC-ESI-Orbitrap-MS/MS analysis showed 101 compounds, mainly flavonoids, hydrolysable tannins, coumarins, and phenolic acid derivatives. The aqueous acetone extracts had the highest phenolic content (up to 86.94 mg GAE per g, roots) and the strongest radical scavenging activity (roots: 277.80 mg TE per g in DPPH, 685.30 mg TE per g in ABTS). The same root extract was the best tyrosinase inhibitor (71.16 mg KAE per g), and the root water extract gave the lowest CA I IC50 (42.51 µg mL−1). Target prediction for 19 annotated constituents (proposed structures) returned 105 human targets, and disease enrichment repeatedly pointed to neuropathic and pain-related phenotypes. Neuropathic pain was therefore selected as the single disease context for all subsequent network, transcriptomic and machine-learning analyses. Three of these targets overlapped with neuropathic pain genes: TRPV1, SCN9A, and OPRL1. TRPV1 alone reached an out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.864, close to the three-gene model (0.868), a difference that is not meaningful. It was also retained in all 50 outer-fold ElasticNet fits, against 12% for OPRL1 and 2% for SCN9A. These transcriptomic analyses show an association with neuropathic pain in a small nerve cohort only; the effect was not replicated in blood (GSE126611) and does not validate an action of the compounds on these targets. In molecular dynamics simulations of five acetylcholinesterase-ligand complexes, three complexes (C1, C3 and C5) showed limited structural deviation and sustained protein–ligand contacts, whereas C4 and, in particular, C2 showed larger conformational changes. Hydrogen-bond analysis indicated dynamic intermolecular interactions, while PCA and free-energy landscape analyses revealed distinct conformational states across the complexes. These findings provide hypothesis-generating structural information that complements the interaction profiles identified by molecular docking. Therefore, E. macroclada may be a promising source of bioactive compounds, providing a basis for further studies.
